topic_candidates.title: Steve Jobs vs Touchscreen MacBooks: Who Was Right?
topic_candidates.query: Steve Jobs touchscreen laptops ergonomically terrible arm fatigue Apple 2010 new MacBook Pro 2026
topic_candidates.brief: Open with the viral contrast: Steve Jobs rejected touchscreen laptops because he said using a vertical screen would make your arm tired, yet Apple now sells one. Reconstruct the original ergonomic argument, then explain what changed in the hardware and software. The final question is not whether Apple contradicted Jobs, but whether Apple found a limited use for touch without turning the Mac into an iPad.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: A report on Jobs’s 2010 comments describes his objection as ergonomic fatigue from repeatedly reaching toward a vertical laptop display. Apple’s 2026 announcement now positions touch as an occasional companion to the keyboard and trackpad, with a redesigned hinge and touch-specific workflows. ([tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/laptops/apple-launches-new-macbook-with-touchscreen-and-oled-starts-at-usd2-899?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: The Verge — “Steve Jobs on touchscreen MacBooks”; 7.6x channel average, 38,861 views per hour
topic_candidates.science_angle: The central engineering issue is posture and torque: holding an arm forward against gravity creates fatigue, so the usefulness of touch depends on short interactions, screen angle and whether the trackpad remains the primary control.
